items.paragraph: Screening programmes are usually judged by how many cases of disease they find, and by that measure more sensitive tests always look better. options.A: Because routine courtesies seldom express what speakers really feel, people ought to keep such phrases for occasions on which their words match their inner states.
options.B: Polite formulas are valuable chiefly because they let people conceal contempt and keep strangers at a distance, which allows social life to continue without open conflict.

items.paragraph: Critics of everyday courtesy often complain that phrases such as 'how are you' or 'thank you so much' are empty, since the speaker rarely wants a medical report and is seldom overwhelmed with gratitude. The complaint assumes that words are sincere only when they report an inner state. But many polite formulas are not reports at all; they are moves in a shared routine, closer to a handshake than to a confession. Their meaning lies in being offered and returned, and their omission is noticed precisely because nobody expects them to carry personal feeling. To call them insincere is therefore to judge them by a standard they never claimed to meet. This does not mean that every courteous word is innocent: a formula can be used to hold someone at a distance or to cover contempt. Yet that misuse is possible only because the routine itself has a recognised social meaning.

items.paragraph: The phrase 'the Silk Road' suggests a single highway along which caravans carried silk from China to Rome. The reality was a shifting web of routes, by land and sea, along which most goods travelled only short distances before changing hands. Few merchants made the whole journey; a bale might pass through a dozen markets, each trader knowing only the next stage. Silk was one commodity among many, and ideas, technologies and diseases moved along the same paths. The single name is convenient, but it can make a loose and long-lived network sound like a planned route.

items.paragraph: When a public project runs far over budget, the most common argument for finishing it is that too much has already been spent to stop. (1) On that view, the only relevant question is whether the benefits still to come exceed the costs still to come. If they do not, every further rupee is wasted, however painful it is to admit that the earlier ones were wasted too. (2) Yet the charge of sunk cost reasoning can be levelled too quickly. (3) Part of what has been spent may have bought something real, such as cleared land, foundations or trained staff, that makes completion cheaper than starting afresh elsewhere. In that case the earlier spending matters, not because it has been spent but because of what it has left behind. (4) The careful test, then, is to ask what the remaining work will cost and yield, counting the past only through its useful remains.

options.A: When the actions in a program cannot be reversed, people become cautious, read the instructions first and use only the operations they already trust.

options.C: By making mistakes cheap to reverse, the undo command encourages users to experiment, and since people learn programs largely by trial and error, this tolerance of errors also helps them learn.

items.paragraph: The undo command looks like a minor convenience, but it changes how people use software. When every action can be reversed, users explore: they try an unfamiliar menu, apply a filter just to see what it does, delete a paragraph to judge whether the essay reads better without it. Where actions are permanent, the same users grow cautious, read instructions first and stick to the few operations they already trust. Undo, in other words, lowers the cost of a mistake, and when mistakes are cheap, experimenting becomes rational. Much of what people learn about a program they learn by just such trial and error, so a design that forgives errors also turns out to be one that teaches.

options.A: Planners should build bypasses only around towns whose shops depend on lingering visitors, and should keep through traffic in towns that serve passing motorists.
options.B: A bypass harms businesses that served passing motorists but may help those depending on visitors who linger in a quieter centre, so early losses poorly predict the outcome.
options.C: Building a bypass around a small town eventually improves trade for all the businesses on its old main road, once the early losses from passing motorists are recovered.
options.D: Shopkeepers are right to fear bypasses, since the trade lost from passing motorists in the first months after opening usually proves permanent for the town.

items.paragraph: When a bypass takes through traffic away from a small town, shopkeepers on the old main road often predict ruin, and in the first months after it opens some of them do lose trade from passing motorists. Yet the longer story is frequently different. Freed from heavy lorries, the main street grows quieter and safer to walk along, and the visitors who now stop do so because they mean to, staying longer than the drivers who once paused for fuel. Businesses that served passing traffic, such as filling stations and roadside cafes, tend to suffer most, while those that depend on people lingering may gain. Whether a town is helped or harmed thus depends on which kind of trade it lived on, and the early losses are a poor guide to the eventual result.
